challenges.boundary: Online public goods game; about 1,200 US participants saw tight, loose, or polarized distributions of earlier players' contributions.

follow.a: They played a two-player public goods game. Each could contribute up to four tokens; contributions were multiplied by 1.4 and shared.
About 1,200 US participants recruited on Prolific, representative by age, gender, and ethnicity.

follow.q: How did polarized norms change choices?
follow.a: Most people picked extreme contributions, which carry more strategic risk than middle options.

challenges.title: Loose rules, varied choices
challenges.scene: Colleagues see highly variable peer behavior rather than a tight shared pattern.
challenges.question: What tends to happen to their own behavior in the studied settings?
options: Their choices clustered on the average
Their choices split into two camps
challenges.answerTitle: Looser norms, wider responses
challenges.explain: Loose norm distributions generated greater behavioral variation in the experiments.
challenges.implication: Where peer behavior varies widely, state expected conduct explicitly, since individual values then drive choices more.
challenges.boundary: Two-player contribution game in which tight, loose, and polarized peer distributions had the same mean.

follow.a: Participants saw a distribution of contributions built from an earlier session, and their partner's contribution was drawn from it.

follow.q: What drives choices when norms are loose?
follow.a: Personal traits mattered more: sucker aversion, free-riding aversion, and personal values shaped decisions more under loose and polarized norms.
Yes. People contributed more when the observed mean was higher (2.4 vs 1.6 tokens), and the mean mattered even more in the polarized condition.

challenges.title: Everyone thinks they are alone
challenges.scene: Team members privately question a practice but believe everybody else supports it.
challenges.question: Students rated their own comfort with campus drinking and the average student’s. What did they report?
options: Peers were more comfortable than they were
Peers were as comfortable as they were
Peers were less comfortable than they were
challenges.answerTitle: Private views and public beliefs diverge
challenges.explain: Pluralistic-ignorance research documents systematic differences between personal attitudes and perceived group attitudes.
challenges.implication: Elicit private views before public discussion.
challenges.boundary: Four studies of college students' own attitudes toward campus alcohol use and their estimates of peers' attitudes.

follow.a: College students, across four studies, who rated their own comfort with campus drinking and estimated the average student's comfort.
In a study that followed students over a semester, men shifted their attitudes toward the norm they mistakenly perceived. Women did not.

follow.q: What did feeling out of step cost?
follow.a: Students who saw themselves as deviant felt more alienated from campus, even though that deviance was illusory.

study.design: Four studies, one following students over a semester

challenges.title: The supposedly united group
challenges.scene: Members of a political group agree on its headline position. A richer measure asks about views within that group.
challenges.question: What did the published norm-drawing study reveal?
challenges.answerTitle: Groups are less monolithic
challenges.explain: The study recovered divergence between parties and multiple co-existing views within each party, more so among Republicans than Democrats on most issues.
challenges.implication: Before engaging a stakeholder group, map the distinct views inside it and estimate each view's share.
challenges.boundary: One incentivized online survey of 996 US respondents on seven political issues, compared with a standard single-norm measure.

follow.a: 996 US respondents on Prolific, stratified by age, gender, and political orientation.
Abortion, same-sex rights, marijuana legalization, federal spending, gun violence, immigration, and energy investments.
Respondents sketch the views different subgroups might hold and estimate the share holding each. Pay depends on how close their guesses come.

challenges.title: Which network spreads change?
challenges.scene: In an online health community, researchers built networks that were either clustered (neighbors share neighbors) or random (more long-range ties), then seeded a health behavior.
challenges.question: Is this what the study found?
challenges.answerTitle: Reinforcement can beat reach
challenges.explain: In the experimental networks, clustered ties supported diffusion of a health behavior requiring social reinforcement.
challenges.implication: Launch hard-to-adopt practices inside tightly connected teams, so each person hears about them from several colleagues.
challenges.boundary: 1,528 anonymous online participants in constructed networks deciding whether to register for a health forum.

follow.q: How much farther did it spread?
follow.a: The behavior reached 53.77% of people in clustered networks, against 38.26% in random networks.
Diffusion in clustered networks was more than four times faster than in random ones.
Yes. Fewer than 15% of adopters who got one signal returned to the forum, against over 30% of those who got two.

forecast.claim: The behavior spread farther through networks with random long ties than through clustered networks with redundant ties.

challenges.title: Who gets the floor?
challenges.scene: Two project groups have similar individual talent. One shares discussion evenly; the other is dominated by a few voices.
challenges.question: Which group feature predicted performance across many different tasks?
challenges.answerTitle: Air time matters
challenges.explain: The group-intelligence study linked collective performance to social sensitivity and conversational turn-taking.
challenges.implication: In team meetings, track who speaks and rotate the floor so one or two members do not dominate.
challenges.boundary: Correlational lab studies of 699 people in groups of two to five; turn-taking was measured with badges in some groups.

follow.q: What tasks did the groups do?
follow.a: A range including visual puzzles, brainstorming, collective moral judgments, and negotiating over limited resources.

follow.q: Did individual IQ predict group performance?
follow.a: Not significantly. The group factor correlated r = .19 with average and r = .27 with maximum member intelligence, neither significant.

follow.q: Why did having more women help?
follow.a: The effect appeared largely mediated by social sensitivity, on which women scored higher.

study.n: 699 people in groups of two to five

challenges.title: Identical résumé, different name
challenges.scene: In a field experiment, comparable résumés were assigned names signaling different racial identities.
challenges.question: Approximately how much higher was the callback rate for White-sounding names?
challenges.answerTitle: 50% more callbacks
challenges.explain: The field experiment found a large gap in callbacks associated with names, holding résumé content constant.
challenges.implication: Run periodic paired-résumé audits of your own screening, comparing callbacks for identical profiles with different names.
challenges.boundary: Fictitious résumés sent to sales, administrative, clerical, and customer-service ads in Boston and Chicago, 2001 to 2002.

follow.a: A White name was worth about as much as eight additional years of experience in callbacks.

follow.q: Did a stronger résumé close the gap?
follow.a: No. Better credentials raised callbacks much less for African-American names than for White names.
No. Neither employers using that label nor federal contractors showed a smaller gap.

estimate.label: Callback advantage (%)

study.n: Nearly 5,000 résumés sent to over 1,300 job ads

challenges.title: Remove the signal
challenges.scene: Orchestra auditions begin concealing candidates’ identity behind screens.
challenges.question: What was the weight of the evidence?
options: Women more likely to advance and be hired
challenges.answerTitle: Screens helped reduce bias
challenges.explain: The study found evidence of increased female advancement and hiring, while noting imprecise and some opposing estimates.
challenges.implication: Hide names and other identity cues in early screening rounds, then compare pass rates by group before and after.
challenges.boundary: Audition records from major US symphony orchestras that adopted screens, mostly in the 1970s and 1980s.

follow.a: In the working-paper version, the screen raised by 50% the chance a woman advanced out of certain preliminary rounds, and raised her chance of winning the final round severalfold.

follow.q: How much of the rise in women does it explain?
follow.a: Blind auditions explain 30% to 55% of the increase in women among new hires, by the working-paper estimates.
With actual audition records, comparing the same musicians across auditions with and without a screen.

study.design: Panel of audition records (individual fixed effects)
study.n: Musicians auditioning at major US orchestras

challenges.title: Why did they stay away?
challenges.scene: Two colleagues from different groups both want more contact but each reads the other’s hesitation as disinterest.
challenges.question: What did intergroup-contact studies observe?
options: Reliable knowledge of the other’s motives
challenges.answerTitle: The misreading can be mutual
challenges.explain: Participants attributed their own avoidance to fear of being rejected because of their race, but the other group's avoidance to lack of interest.
challenges.implication: Have managers make the first cross-group introduction, so neither side has to risk reaching out first.
challenges.boundary: Seven studies of White and Black participants' interest in interracial contact and how they explained avoidance.

follow.a: White and Black participants, across seven studies.
Both groups privately wanted more contact, yet each wrongly believed the other group did not.

follow.q: Did the researchers go beyond attitudes?
follow.a: Yes. One study examined the behavioral consequences of the bias, and a final study tested a way to reduce it based on the extended contact hypothesis.

challenges.title: Is loss aversion a law?
challenges.scene: A workshop leader says: “Losses always hurt more than equal gains feel good.”
challenges.question: Which TWO statements fit the loss-aversion evidence?
options: Loss aversion can reverse in experiments
The distributions of outcomes can matter
Every loss must hurt twice as much as a matching gain
challenges.answerTitle: It is not a universal law
challenges.explain: Experiments have found that apparent loss aversion can disappear or reverse when distributions change.
challenges.implication: Before applying a 2:1 loss-aversion rule to pricing, test how customers respond to the gains and losses they actually face.
challenges.boundary: Accept-or-reject choices on 50/50 money gambles, mostly hypothetical, with Mechanical Turk workers and Warwick students.

follow.a: People accepted or rejected 50/50 gambles offering a gain and a loss. The researchers varied the ranges from which gains and losses were drawn.
Three online experiments with Mechanical Turk workers (323 to 401 analyzed) using hypothetical gambles, and one lab study with 82 Warwick participants playing for real money.
It is contested. Andre and de Langhe (2021) showed the conditions used different gambles; comparing only shared gambles removes the pattern.

study.n: 1,106 MTurk workers and 82 lab participants analyzed

challenges.title: Hate or love?
challenges.scene: Across a series of online experiments, Trump supporters and opponents report feeling closer to their own side and also make costly choices toward the other side.
challenges.question: Which distinction emerged across experiments?
options: Love showed in feelings, hate in behavior
Hate showed in feelings, love in behavior
Both showed in feelings, not in behavior
challenges.answerTitle: The domains diverged
challenges.explain: The published study found ingroup love in perceived closeness, but outgroup hate in behavioral outcomes.
challenges.implication: When teams distrust each other, share evidence of the other side's actual cooperation, since pessimistic expectations drove the hostility.
challenges.boundary: Incentivized behavioral experiments with US Trump supporters and opponents, plus a sports-identity comparison.

follow.q: How large was the evidence base?
follow.a: Five preregistered studies with 15 behavioral experiments and over 8,600 participants.
Grim expectations about how cooperative the other side would be, rather than a flat refusal to cooperate across factions.
In the working-paper version, a dictator game where people could give or take money, and a public goods game that also measured beliefs about others.

challenges.title: When a nudge is not enough
challenges.scene: A leader offers prosocial defaults and normative messages to participants divided by political identity.
challenges.question: Which TWO observations characterize the tested interventions?
options: Defaults completely removed the identity gap
challenges.answerTitle: General improvement, persistent gap
challenges.explain: In the paper, tested defaults and norm nudges raised prosociality but did not close measured polarization gaps.
challenges.implication: Track between-group gaps as a separate metric when testing interventions, since average cooperation can rise while the gap stays.
challenges.boundary: Default and norm nudges tested in incentivized giving and cooperation games with US Trump supporters and opponents.

follow.a: A default nudge and a norm nudge that gave descriptive information about others' behavior.
In the working-paper version, a sports-identity comparison also showed an ingroup-outgroup gap in giving, though not in cooperation.

follow.q: Why might nudges miss the gap?
follow.a: The gap traced to grim expectations about the other side's cooperativeness, which raising overall giving does not address.

challenges.title: The missing distribution
challenges.scene: Two departments report identical average appropriateness ratings. One is unified; the other contains opposing camps.
challenges.question: Two teams give the same average answer on what conduct is acceptable. How do you see whether their norms differ?
options: Keep each person’s view, not just the mean
Ask each manager to describe the norm
challenges.answerTitle: Keep the whole distribution
challenges.explain: The published measurement paper describes how eliciting norm-belief distributions can reveal disagreement hidden by mean or mode.
challenges.implication: In culture surveys, ask each person how views are spread across colleagues, not only what the typical view is.
challenges.boundary: A short methods paper presenting an incentive-compatible survey tool that measures each person's perceived norm distribution.

follow.q: What do standard norm measures capture?
follow.a: The average or most frequent behavior or opinion in a given context.
The method is incentive-compatible, so respondents are rewarded for reporting their real beliefs about how views are spread.
Yes. The paper comes with ready-made Qualtrics software.

challenges.title: Same numbers, other frame
challenges.scene: A disease will kill 600 people. Framed as lives saved, 72% chose a sure plan (200 saved) over a gamble. Others saw the same plans framed as deaths: 400 die for sure, or a one-third chance nobody dies.
challenges.question: In the deaths frame, what share chose the gamble?
challenges.answerTitle: 78% gambled once the frame was losses
challenges.explain: With identical outcomes, 72% chose the sure option when it was framed as lives saved; 78% chose the gamble when the same options were framed as deaths.
challenges.implication: In investment memos, state each option's outcomes as both gains and losses before the team decides.
challenges.boundary: Stanford and UBC students choosing between hypothetical public-health programs in a classroom questionnaire.

follow.a: Students at Stanford and the University of British Columbia, in brief classroom questionnaires: 152 saw the lives-saved version and 155 the deaths version.

follow.q: Do experts fall for it too?
follow.a: Yes. The authors report the same reversal in other groups, including university faculty and physicians.

follow.q: Why does the frame flip choices?
follow.a: People tend to avoid risk when outcomes are described as gains and to take risk when they are described as losses.

estimate.label: Share choosing the gamble in the deaths frame

challenges.title: Who should have the final say?
challenges.scene: You are designing workflows for three AI-supported tasks. A meta-analysis of 106 experiments shows when humans plus AI beat either one working alone.
challenges.question: For each task, who should do the work?

tasks.text: Flag fake hotel reviews: AI is 73% accurate, staff 55%
tasks.why: In this example the human-AI team scored 69%, below the AI alone at 73%.

tasks.text: Classify bird photos: staff are 81% accurate, AI 73%
tasks.why: Here the human-AI team reached 90%, beating both humans and AI alone.

challenges.answerTitle: Combine only where humans beat the AI
challenges.explain: Across 370 effect sizes, human-AI teams did worse than the best performer alone (g = -0.23). They gained when humans beat the AI (g = 0.46) and lost when the AI was better (g = -0.54).
challenges.implication: Benchmark humans and AI separately before adding a human review layer; skip that layer where the AI alone is clearly stronger.
challenges.boundary: Covers experiments published January 2020 to June 2023; averages span very different tasks, so they are no rule for one workflow.

follow.q: Do humans with AI beat humans alone?
follow.a: Yes. Against humans alone, human-AI systems performed better (g = 0.64). The losses appear only against the better of the two.
Decision tasks, where people choose from a fixed set of options, showed losses (g = -0.27). Creation tasks trended positive (g = 0.19, not significant).

follow.q: Where do the review and bird numbers come from?
follow.a: Both come from Cabrera, Perer and Hong (2023), which the authors discuss to show how relative skill drives synergy.

challenges.title: Give them a small dial
challenges.scene: In an incentivized task, people forecast students' math percentiles. They may use an imperfect model that outperforms human forecasts, but each group gets different rules for adjusting it.
challenges.question: Rank the groups by share who chose to use the model.
options: Could adjust each forecast by up to 10
Could adjust each forecast by up to 2
Could not change the model at all
challenges.answerTitle: Any control beats none; size barely matters
challenges.explain: In Study 2, 47% used the unchangeable model versus 68% to 71% when they could adjust it by 2, 5 or 10 percentiles. The two adjustable groups did not differ meaningfully, so their order is not scored.
challenges.implication: Let staff make small, bounded adjustments to model outputs instead of mandating the outputs unchanged.
challenges.boundary: Online and lab forecasting of student test percentiles with small bonuses; workplace accountability and long-term use were not studied.

follow.a: No. Because more people used the model, participants who could modify it forecast more accurately as a result, the authors report.
Also 71%, the same as the 10-percentile limit. More freedom did not raise uptake.
Yes. Being able to modify the model raised satisfaction, belief that the model was superior, and willingness to use algorithms for later forecasts.

challenges.title: Same jail rate, less crime
challenges.scene: Judges decide whether defendants await trial at home or in jail, partly by predicting crime risk. Researchers train a machine-learning model on past cases and simulate letting it rank defendants.
challenges.question: Holding the jailing rate fixed, how much could crime fall?

estimate.label: Maximum crime reduction at the same jailing rate

challenges.answerTitle: Up to 24.7% less crime
challenges.explain: Simulations showed crime reductions up to 24.7% with no change in jailing rates, or jailing cuts up to 41.9% with no rise in crime.
challenges.implication: Audit high-volume screening decisions with a prediction model and estimate how many errors you could cut at today's approval rate.
challenges.boundary: These are policy simulations on past bail cases, not a deployed system; crime outcomes exist only for released defendants.

study.design: Machine-learning policy simulation on court records

follow.q: Couldn't the model just copy judges' choices?
follow.a: Crime is observed only for defendants judges released. The authors use methods such as quasi-random assignment of cases to judges to compare fairly.
The authors report these gains can be achieved while also reducing racial disparities.

follow.q: Is there another way to use the gain?
follow.a: Yes. Hold crime constant and jail fewer people: jailing could fall up to 41.9% with no increase in crime.

challenges.title: The formula versus the expert
challenges.scene: A meta-analysis compares expert clinicians' predictions about human health and behavior with predictions from statistical formulas.
challenges.question: On average, how much more accurate were the formulas?

estimate.label: Average accuracy advantage of formulas over experts

challenges.answerTitle: About 10% more accurate
challenges.explain: Across 136 studies, formulas were about 10% more accurate on average. Experts were substantially more accurate in only 6% to 16% of studies.
challenges.implication: For repeated predictions from structured data, make a validated scoring rule the default and log every expert override.
challenges.boundary: Studies of clinical and behavioral prediction up to 2000 using statistical formulas, not modern AI; many studies showed ties.

follow.a: No. The formula advantage held across judgment tasks, types of judges, judges' experience and types of data.

follow.q: Do interviews give experts an edge?
follow.a: The reverse. Clinical predictions did relatively worse when predictors included clinical interview data.

follow.q: How often did formulas win clearly?
follow.a: Formulas substantially outperformed experts in 33% to 47% of studies. In many others the two were about equally accurate.

challenges.title: The wrong target variable
challenges.scene: A health system uses a widely sold algorithm to choose patients for an extra-care program. It predicts future health-care costs and treats high predicted cost as high need.
challenges.question: Why were Black patients flagged less than equally sick White patients?
options: Race was an input to the model
Less is spent on Black patients at equal need
Black patients had fewer chronic illnesses
The model had too little training data

dag.alt: Health need and race both affect spending. The risk score is trained to predict spending, so lower spending on Black patients lowers their scores at the same need.

chart.note: Share of Black patients receiving additional help. Values reported in Obermeyer et al. 2019, abstract.

challenges.answerTitle: Cost was a biased proxy for need
challenges.explain: Less money is spent caring for Black patients, so predicted cost understated their need. Removing the disparity would raise their share of extra help from 17.7% to 46.5%.
challenges.implication: Before deploying a model, confirm its target measures what you care about, and audit outcomes by group at equal scores.
challenges.boundary: One widely used commercial algorithm in US health care; the size of the bias depends on spending gaps in each system.

study.design: Audit of a deployed commercial algorithm

follow.a: Reformulating the algorithm so it no longer used costs as a proxy for needs eliminated the racial bias in predicting who needs extra care.
At a given risk score, Black patients were sicker than White patients, and the bias cut the number of Black patients identified for extra care by more than half.

follow.q: Why did cost seem a sensible target?
follow.a: The authors note that health-care cost appears to be an effective proxy for health on many measures, which made the problem easy to miss.

challenges.title: When managers overrule the test
challenges.scene: Fifteen firms hiring low-skilled service workers introduce a job test that scores applicants. Managers can still hire against its recommendations.
challenges.question: Is this what the study found?

forecast.claim: Managers who hired against test recommendations more often ended up with better average hires.

challenges.answerTitle: Overruling the test went with worse hires
challenges.explain: Comparing managers with similar applicant pools, those who appeared to hire against test recommendations ended up with worse average hires.
challenges.implication: Track override rates by manager, compare outcomes of overridden hires, and require a written reason for each override.
challenges.boundary: Low-skilled service jobs at 15 firms adopting job testing; professional and creative roles were not studied.

follow.a: The authors conclude managers often overrule test recommendations because they are biased or mistaken, not mainly because they hold better information.

follow.q: What tradeoff does the firm face?
follow.a: More weight on test scores can cut bias and error but may discard useful private information held by managers. Here the first effect dominated.
The authors compared managers facing similar applicant pools, so differences in overrides were not just differences in who applied.

challenges.title: Spot the AI profile
challenges.scene: Readers see self-descriptions written for job, hospitality and dating profiles. Some were written by people, others by an AI language model.
challenges.question: Is this what the study found?

forecast.claim: People identified which self-descriptions were AI-written clearly better than chance.

challenges.answerTitle: Detection was at chance: 50 to 52%
challenges.explain: Across experiments with 4,600 participants, people identified the source with only 50 to 52% accuracy, relying on cues like first-person pronouns and family topics.
challenges.implication: Do not count on reviewers to spot AI-written applications or reviews; set disclosure rules and verify claims directly.
challenges.boundary: Short self-presentations in professional, hospitality and dating contexts, judged by online participants; other text types were not tested.

follow.a: No. In the dating context half the participants were offered a $3 accuracy bonus, with no difference in performance.

follow.q: Can AI text seem more human than human?
follow.a: Yes. Text optimized against people's cues was judged human 65.7% of the time, versus 51.7% for real human text.
First-person pronouns, contractions and family topics were read as signs of a human writer, but they did not reliably indicate one.

challenges.title: Who argues your case?
challenges.scene: In 10-minute online debates on assigned topics, people faced either a human or GPT-4. Some opponents also received basic demographic details about the person they debated.
challenges.question: Split a persuasion pilot budget across four opponent types.

allocate.label: Pilot budget
allocate.valueName: change in odds of higher post-debate agreement vs human-human debates (non-significant changes count as zero)

challenges.answerTitle: Personalized GPT-4 was most persuasive
challenges.explain: Versus human-human debates, personalized GPT-4 raised the odds of higher post-debate agreement by 81.2%. GPT-4 without profiles and personalized humans showed no significant effect.
challenges.implication: Treat customer data fed to persuasive AI as a governed input; review consent and disclosure before using it in sales.
challenges.boundary: Short structured online debates with assigned positions and basic demographics; long-run commercial persuasion was not tested.

follow.q: How often did personalized GPT-4 win?
follow.a: In pairs where the two sides were not equally persuasive, personalized GPT-4 was more persuasive 64.4% of the time.

follow.q: Could people tell they faced an AI?
follow.a: Often. Participants identified AI opponents in about three of four cases; for human opponents, identification was near chance (52.0%).

follow.q: Did humans use the profile well?
follow.a: No. Humans given the same demographic details were not significantly more persuasive (-15.7%, P = 0.38).

challenges.title: The cost of an AI label
challenges.scene: A news site plans to tag headlines 'AI-generated' whenever AI was involved, including true headlines its staff wrote and checked.
challenges.question: Is this what the study found?
challenges.answerTitle: Less believed and less shared
challenges.explain: Across 4,976 participants, the label cut perceived accuracy and sharing whether headlines were true or false, human- or AI-made. The effect was three times smaller than a 'false' label.
challenges.implication: If you label AI use, state what the AI did; vague labels read as full automation and penalize accurate content.
challenges.boundary: Headlines shown to US and UK online participants; the penalty disappeared when labels came with weak or medium definitions of AI involvement.

follow.a: Readers expected AI-labeled headlines to be written entirely by AI. Without a definition, they leaned toward assuming full automation.
In Study 2 the labels had no significant effect when readers got weak or medium definitions. The penalty remained with no definition or a strong one.
Yes. Human-made headlines wrongly labeled as AI-generated were also rated lower.

forecast.claim: Labeling headlines “AI-generated” lowered belief in them even when the headlines were true and written by people.

challenges.title: Make them think first
challenges.scene: People make decisions with help from an AI that is usually right but sometimes wrong. Designers compare plain AI explanations with designs that force users to engage before relying on the AI.
challenges.question: Which design best cut agreement with wrong AI advice?
options: Forcing users to engage before relying
challenges.answerTitle: Forcing functions worked, but users disliked them
challenges.explain: Among 199 participants, cognitive forcing designs significantly reduced overreliance compared with simple explainable-AI designs. The most effective designs received the least favorable ratings.
challenges.implication: On high-stakes calls, have reviewers record their own judgment before AI output appears, and plan for user pushback.
challenges.boundary: One online decision task; benefits were larger for people higher in Need for Cognition, who enjoy effortful thinking.

follow.a: Participants higher in Need for Cognition, who enjoy effortful thinking, benefited more from the interventions.
People gave the least favorable ratings to the designs that reduced overreliance most, a tradeoff between performance and user preference.
Three interventions built to compel people to engage more thoughtfully with the AI's suggestions and explanations before relying on them.

challenges.title: Your spouse versus the algorithm
challenges.scene: People rate a set of jokes. Then a stranger, a friend, a family member or a recommender system predicts which new jokes they will find funny.
challenges.question: Which TWO findings did the study report?
options: The algorithm beat strangers, friends and family
Spouses and family beat the algorithm
People preferred relying on human recommenders
People found the algorithm easier to understand
challenges.answerTitle: More accurate, yet people preferred humans
challenges.explain: Recommender systems outperformed strangers, friends and family at predicting joke ratings. People still resisted relying on them, partly because human recommendations felt easier to understand.
challenges.implication: When launching a recommender, explain in plain terms why it suggests each item; accuracy alone will not win adoption.
challenges.boundary: Joke preferences, a taste domain where humans have many advantages; product or hiring recommendations were not tested.

study.design: Experiments comparing human and algorithmic recommenders

follow.a: The authors chose a domain where human recommenders have many advantages, which makes the algorithm's win a hard test.
Partly because they believed the human recommendation process was easier to understand than the algorithm's.
Accuracy is not enough. Recommender systems must also be understood if people are to rely on them.

challenges.title: The ad that skipped women
challenges.scene: A firm runs a gender-neutral ad promoting STEM careers and lets the platform's algorithm deliver it cost-effectively. Fewer women than men end up seeing it.
challenges.question: What best explains the gap?
options: The algorithm learned women click less
Showing ads to young women costs more
The advertiser targeted men by mistake
challenges.answerTitle: Young women cost more to reach
challenges.explain: Younger women are a prized audience and more expensive to show ads to, so a cost-optimizing algorithm delivered fewer STEM ads to them through crowding out.
challenges.implication: Audit who actually sees your recruiting ads and set reach targets by group rather than pure cost optimization.
challenges.boundary: One field test of STEM career ads, with the same pattern on other major platforms; it studies ad delivery, not hiring outcomes.

follow.a: No. The ad was intended to be gender neutral; the gap came from an algorithm that simply optimized cost-effectiveness.
The authors report the same regularity extends to other major digital platforms.

follow.q: What does crowding out mean here?
follow.a: Other advertisers value younger women highly, so reaching them costs more, and a cost-minimizing campaign reaches fewer of them.

challenges.title: Do customers notice the AI?
challenges.scene: A firm rolls out a generative-AI assistant that suggests replies to its customer-support agents, in stages across 5,172 agents.
challenges.question: Is this what the study found?

forecast.claim: After agents got AI assistance, customers became less likely to ask for a manager.

challenges.answerTitle: Customers got politer and escalated less
challenges.explain: With AI assistance, customers were more polite and less likely to ask to speak to a manager, alongside a 15% average rise in issues resolved per hour.
challenges.implication: Track escalation rates and customer tone in AI pilots; part of the payoff may show up in supervisors' time.
challenges.boundary: One firm's customer-support chat operation with a staggered rollout, not random assignment of agents.

follow.a: Gains were largest for moderately rare problems, where agents had less experience but the system still had enough training data.
The authors find AI assistance facilitated worker learning and improved English fluency, especially among international agents.
The authors report AI assistance improved the experience of work along several dimensions.

challenges.title: How much faster with GPT-4?
challenges.scene: BCG consultants work on 18 realistic tasks for a fictional footwear company, such as new product ideas and a press release. Some are randomly given GPT-4.
challenges.question: How much faster did consultants with AI finish?

estimate.label: Speed gain on inside-frontier tasks

challenges.answerTitle: 25.1% faster, with more tasks done
challenges.explain: Consultants with GPT-4 completed 12.2% more tasks and worked 25.1% faster. Graded quality rose 29.9% with GPT-4 alone and 33.9% with prompt training.
challenges.implication: Pilot AI on drafting and ideation first, and measure speed, completion and blind-graded quality together.
challenges.boundary: One firm's consultants on designed tasks for a fictional company; on a task outside the frontier, AI users were less often correct.

follow.a: The bottom-half-skill consultants benefited most, though above-average consultants also benefited meaningfully.
Somewhat. Quality rose 33.9% with a prompt-engineering overview versus 29.9% with GPT-4 alone.
Yes. On a task built to sit outside AI's frontier, correctness fell from about 84.5% without AI to 70.6% and 60% with it.

challenges.title: Who gets the assistant first?
challenges.scene: You run a 400-agent support center and can license a generative-AI reply assistant for 100 agents this quarter. Your goal is the largest gain in issues resolved.
challenges.question: Which agents should get the first licenses?
challenges.answerTitle: Start with less experienced agents
challenges.explain: In a rollout to 5,172 agents, issues resolved per hour rose 15% on average. Less experienced and lower-skilled agents improved speed and quality; top agents gained little.
challenges.implication: Target early licenses at newer and lower-performing staff, and report gains by tenure tier.
challenges.boundary: Customer-support chat at one firm; gains were largest on moderately rare problems where the system had enough training data.

follow.a: The most experienced and highest-skilled agents saw only small gains in speed and small declines in quality.
Issues resolved per hour, which rose 15% on average with access to the assistant.

follow.q: Why do the exact tier gains not appear here?
follow.a: Subgroup percentages were not in the journal text we could read, so this item uses the direction the abstract reports.

challenges.title: Will your stars get better too?
challenges.scene: Licenses now extend to your most experienced, highest-skilled agents. A director predicts the assistant will lift their work just as it did for newer agents.
challenges.question: Is this what the study found?

forecast.claim: For the most experienced, highest-skilled agents, AI assistance improved both speed and quality.

challenges.answerTitle: Top agents: slightly faster, slightly lower quality
challenges.explain: In the same rollout, the most experienced and highest-skilled agents saw small gains in speed and small declines in quality.
challenges.implication: Let top performers tune or skip suggestions, and monitor their quality scores after rollout.
challenges.boundary: One firm's support chat; the declines for top agents were small, and other occupations may differ.

follow.a: Yes. Less experienced and lower-skilled agents improved both the speed and quality of their output.

follow.q: Does the AI help experts at all?
follow.a: Slightly. They saw small gains in speed, offset by small declines in quality.
Customers were more polite and less likely to ask to speak to a manager.

challenges.title: Which tasks go to GPT-4?
challenges.scene: Next, your strategy team gets GPT-4. Their work ranges from brainstorming product ideas to a brand recommendation that hinges on details buried in interview notes.
challenges.question: Assign each task.

tasks.text: Propose ten product ideas for an underserved market
tasks.why: Inside the frontier, consultants with GPT-4 finished 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, with higher graded quality.

tasks.text: Draft press-release copy for the new product
tasks.why: This was one of the inside-frontier tasks, where AI users produced higher-quality work.

tasks.text: Pick the brand to grow from interview notes and spreadsheets
tasks.why: On this outside-frontier task, correctness fell from about 84.5% without AI to 70.6% and 60% with GPT-4.

challenges.answerTitle: Use AI inside the frontier, not outside
challenges.explain: Inside the frontier, AI users completed 12.2% more tasks and worked 25.1% faster. On the outside-frontier case, correctness fell from about 84.5% to 70.6% and 60%.
challenges.implication: Test each task type for convincing AI errors before rollout; keep humans in charge where those errors appear.
challenges.boundary: One designed outside-frontier task for a fictional company; the frontier moves as models change.

follow.q: Did prompt training help on the hard task?
follow.a: No. The group with a prompt-engineering overview was correct about 60% of the time, below GPT-4 alone at 70.6%.

follow.q: How was the hard task built?
follow.a: Success required a careful review of interview notes that held the key details, then advice to the CEO on which brand held the most growth potential.
758 BCG consultants, randomized to no AI, GPT-4, or GPT-4 with a prompt-engineering overview.

challenges.title: Learning with a crutch
challenges.scene: HR proposes unrestricted ChatGPT-style access in new-hire training. In a related field experiment, high school students practiced math with GPT-4, then took exams without it.
challenges.question: How did unrestricted-AI students score on unaided exams versus controls?

estimate.label: Change in exam grades vs students without AI

challenges.answerTitle: 17% lower on exams without AI
challenges.explain: Practice grades rose 48% with plain GPT-4, but exam grades fell 17% versus students never given access. A tutor version with safeguards showed no measurable exam harm.
challenges.implication: In training, use AI tutors that give hints rather than answers, and test skills without AI before certifying anyone.
challenges.boundary: Nearly 1,000 high school math students in Turkey over four 90-minute sessions; adult workplace training was not tested.

follow.q: What were students doing with it?
follow.a: Most used plain GPT-4 to obtain solutions; the most common message was 'What is the answer?'
No. Students in the plain GPT-4 arm did not perceive that they performed worse or learned less.

follow.q: What did the tutor version change?
follow.a: It added safeguards such as hints instead of answers and teacher-provided solutions. Practice grades rose 127%, and exam scores matched controls.

challenges.title: The lift that wasn't there
challenges.scene: Your agency compares Facebook users who saw your campaign with users who did not. After matching on age and gender, it reports a 222% conversion lift. A randomized holdout ran at the same time.
challenges.question: What lift did the randomized holdout show?
challenges.answerTitle: The experiment found 73%, not 222%
challenges.explain: In Study 4 the randomized lift was 73%, while exact matching on age and gender gave 222% and the naive exposed-versus-unexposed comparison 316%.
challenges.implication: Keep a randomized holdout for major campaigns before trusting matched or platform-reported lift numbers.
challenges.boundary: Fifteen US Facebook campaigns; observational methods sometimes underestimated lift, so the bias does not always run upward.

dag.alt: A random holdout determines ad exposure. Unobserved user activity drives both who sees the ad and who buys, so comparing exposed and unexposed users confounds the ad's effect on purchase.

chart.note: Values reported in Gordon et al. (2019), Study 4.

follow.a: Fifteen US advertising RCTs run at Facebook, covering about 500 million user-experiment observations and 1.6 billion impressions.
No. In half of the studies, the estimated percentage increase in purchases was off by a factor of three across all observational methods.
Mostly, but not always. In some studies they significantly underestimated the randomized lift.

study.design: 15 field RCTs compared with observational methods

challenges.title: The noisy ROI test
challenges.scene: Your CFO wants a randomized test to prove a digital campaign's return before renewing it. Individual customers' weekly sales swing wildly.
challenges.question: Across 25 large ad experiments, how wide was the median ROI confidence interval?

estimate.label: Median width of the ROI confidence interval

challenges.answerTitle: Over 100 percentage points wide
challenges.explain: The median confidence interval on return on investment was over 100 percentage points wide, because individual sales are very noisy relative to ad effects.
challenges.implication: Pool several experiments or measure lower-variance outcomes before asking one test to settle a campaign's ROI.
challenges.boundary: Digital ads for major US retailers and brokerages; the experiments were unbiased, the limit was statistical precision.

follow.a: The 25 experiments represented $2.8 million in digital advertising expenditure.

follow.q: How big would a decisive test be?
follow.a: With a coefficient of variation of sales around 10, which the authors call common, informative experiments can require more than 10 million person-weeks.

follow.q: Does this mean RCTs are useless here?
follow.a: No. Randomization still removes selection bias; the problem is that ad effects are small relative to sales noise, so estimates are imprecise.

study.n: 25 ad campaigns at US retailers and brokerages

challenges.title: Save more, later
challenges.scene: Employees save little for retirement and resist raising contributions now. An adviser offers a plan that commits part of each future pay raise to savings.
challenges.question: Participants started at a 3.5% savings rate. Where were they after four raises?

estimate.label: Average savings rate after four pay raises

challenges.answerTitle: Savings rates rose from 3.5% to 13.6%
challenges.explain: In the first implementation, participants' savings rates increased from 3.5 percent to 13.6 percent over 40 months, and 78 percent of those offered the plan joined.
challenges.implication: Offer a sign-up that raises retirement contributions at each future raise, so take-home pay never falls.
challenges.boundary: Early company implementations with employees who chose to join; not a randomized trial.

follow.a: 78 percent of those offered the plan joined.
Few did. 80 percent of those enrolled remained in it through the fourth pay raise.
Employees commit in advance to allocating part of future salary increases to saving, so the extra saving starts when pay goes up rather than out of current take-home pay.

study.n: Employees offered the plan at the first implementing firm

challenges.title: Your best guess is late
challenges.scene: Senior honors students gave their most realistic date for finishing their thesis, plus a best-case and a worst-case date. Researchers then tracked when they actually finished.
challenges.question: What share finished by their own most realistic date?

estimate.label: Share finishing by their best-guess date

challenges.answerTitle: Fewer than one in three finished on time
challenges.explain: Only 29.7% finished by their best-guess date. On average they predicted 33.9 days and took 55.5 days.
challenges.implication: Set project deadlines from how long similar past projects actually took, not from the team's step-by-step plan.
challenges.boundary: Study 1 tracked 37 psychology honors students on their theses; one task type, one university.

follow.a: Not reliably. Only 48.7% finished by the date they predicted if everything went as poorly as it possibly could.

follow.q: How far off was the average?
follow.a: Students predicted 33.9 days on average; actual completion averaged 55.5 days.
Later studies in the paper point to focusing on plans for the future while discounting past experience with similar tasks.

challenges.title: Shirking from home?
challenges.scene: Ctrip, a 16,000-employee Chinese travel agency, asked call-center staff to volunteer for home working, then randomly assigned volunteers to home or office for nine months.
challenges.question: By how much did home workers' performance change?

estimate.label: Change in performance when working from home

challenges.answerTitle: Performance rose 13%
challenges.explain: Home working led to a 13% performance increase, 9% of it from working more minutes per shift, and attrition roughly halved.
challenges.implication: Pilot remote work on roles with measurable output, assign it randomly, and judge it on output rather than presence.
challenges.boundary: Volunteer call-center staff with easily measured output; home workers' promotion rate, given performance, fell.

follow.q: Where did the gain come from?
follow.a: Nine of the 13 points came from working more minutes per shift; the rest from more calls per minute, which the authors attribute to a quieter, more convenient setting.

follow.q: What happened when it went company-wide?
follow.a: Over half of employees switched their choice, and the gains from working from home almost doubled to 22%, which the authors attribute to learning and selection.
Yes. Conditional on performance, home workers' promotion rate fell.

study.n: Volunteer call-center staff at Ctrip, 9 months

challenges.title: Mine is worth more
challenges.scene: Students were split into three groups. Sellers were given a coffee mug, buyers could buy one, and choosers picked between the mug and cash.
challenges.question: Rank the groups by the median value they placed on the same mug.
challenges.rankLabel: Highest median valuation of the mug
challenges.answerTitle: Owners valued the mug over twice as much
challenges.explain: Median valuations were $7.12 for sellers, $3.12 for choosers and $2.87 for buyers. Choosers face the same trade-off as sellers without owning the mug, so ownership drives the gap.
challenges.implication: When reallocating budgets, territories or assets, expect current holders to value them far above what others would pay.
challenges.boundary: Students trading mugs and pens in classroom markets; tokens with assigned cash values traded as predicted.

follow.a: Yes. While 12.5 trades were expected between buyers and sellers, only three took place.

follow.q: Is it just reluctance to pay?
follow.a: No. Buyers and choosers gave similar values, so the gap reflects reluctance to give up the mug, not reluctance to spend.
No. In Experiment 1, mug markets produced 1 to 4 trades per trial against 11 expected, while induced-value token markets matched predictions.

challenges.title: Who stays with hybrid?
challenges.scene: Trip.com randomized 1,612 engineering, marketing and finance staff. Those with odd-numbered birthdays could work from home on Wednesdays and Fridays; the rest stayed in the office full time.
challenges.question: Rank the groups by how much hybrid work cut their quit rate.
challenges.answerTitle: Quits fell most for women and long commuters
challenges.explain: Hybrid work cut quit rates by one-third overall, with larger drops for women (54%), long commuters (52%) and non-managers (40%). Performance reviews showed no difference over two years.
challenges.implication: Offer two home days a week in high-attrition roles, and track performance reviews to confirm nothing is lost.
challenges.boundary: One Chinese tech firm, six-month trial; the long-commuter reduction (P = 0.062) was not statistically significant.

follow.a: No. Reviews across four half-year periods showed no difference between groups, and equivalence tests supported a null effect.
No evidence of a difference in promotions, and for 653 engineers no difference in daily lines of code.
Yes. Before the trial managers expected a negative effect of 2.6% on average; afterward their estimate turned positive.

challenges.title: The fine that backfired
challenges.scene: Ten Israeli day-care centers tracked late pickups for 20 weeks. In week 5, six centers began fining parents NIS 10 for arriving 10+ minutes late. In week 17 the fine was dropped.
challenges.question: What happened to late pickups after the fine ended?

forecast.claim: After the fine was removed, late pickups stayed at the higher level.

challenges.answerTitle: Lateness nearly doubled and stayed high
challenges.explain: Late pickups rose steadily after the fine, settling almost twice as high as before, and after the fine was removed no reduction occurred.
challenges.implication: Before fining a behavior, ask whether the fine turns a social obligation into a price people will happily pay.
challenges.boundary: A small fine in ten day-care centers over 20 weeks; four control centers showed no change.

follow.a: Yes. In the four centers without a fine, no noticeable change took place after the fourth week, or in any other week.
NIS 10 per child for parents arriving 10 or more minutes late.
The authors observed a steady increase after the fine began, until the rate settled almost twice as large as the initial one.

challenges.title: A photo worth a rate cut
challenges.scene: A consumer lender mailed loan offers to former clients, randomizing the interest rate along with ad content such as a photo, the number of example loans and the offer deadline.
challenges.question: Can ad content move demand as much as price?

forecast.claim: A photo of an attractive woman raised loan demand about as much as a 25% interest-rate cut.

challenges.answerTitle: The photo matched a 25% rate cut
challenges.explain: Showing fewer example loans, not suggesting a particular use, or including a photo of an attractive woman each raised demand about as much as a 25% interest-rate reduction.
challenges.implication: Test creative content against price in randomized offers before giving up margin on discounts.
challenges.boundary: Direct-mail offers of short-term consumer credit in South Africa; one lender's former clients.

follow.a: Fewer example loans, not suggesting a particular use for the loan, and a photo of an attractive woman.
Demand strongly increased with longer deadlines, contrary to the idea that short deadlines help people who procrastinate.
The authors read the evidence as ads persuading by appealing peripherally to intuition rather than to reason.

study.n: Former clients of a consumer lender

challenges.title: Does more choice backfire?
challenges.scene: A famous grocery study found about 30% of shoppers bought jam after a 6-flavor display versus 3% after a 24-flavor display. Your team proposes cutting your product range.
challenges.question: Does choice overload hold on average across studies?

forecast.claim: Across 50 experiments, more options reduced choice or satisfaction on average.

challenges.answerTitle: On average, the effect is near zero
challenges.explain: A meta-analysis of 63 conditions from 50 experiments (5,036 participants) found a mean effect size of virtually zero (D = 0.02), with considerable variance between studies.
challenges.implication: Test a range cut in your own category before assuming fewer options will sell more.
challenges.boundary: Large variance between studies means overload appears in some settings; the average does not say which ones.

follow.q: What did the jam study find exactly?
follow.a: More shoppers stopped at 24 jams (60%) than at 6 (40%), but about 30% of stoppers bought with 6 jams versus 3% with 24.
63 conditions from 50 published and unpublished experiments, with 5,036 participants.

follow.q: So was the jam study wrong?
follow.a: Not necessarily. The meta-analysis found considerable variance between studies, so single results like the jam study coexist with an average near zero.

challenges.title: Sign here first?
challenges.scene: A 2012 PNAS study reported that signing an honesty statement at the top of a form, rather than the bottom, reduced dishonest reports. Government agencies adopted the practice.
challenges.question: Did the sign-first effect hold up?

forecast.claim: A preregistered direct replication with 1,235 people confirmed that signing first reduces dishonesty.

challenges.answerTitle: No effect of signing first
challenges.explain: Across five conceptual replications (n = 4,559) and a preregistered direct replication (n = 1,235), the authors observed no effect of signing first on honest reporting. PNAS retracted the 2012 paper in 2021.
challenges.implication: Before rolling out a published nudge, check for replications and retractions, then pilot it on your own forms.
challenges.boundary: Tests one form-design nudge on experimental self-reports; it does not evaluate honesty interventions in general.

follow.a: The replication team included all five authors of the 2012 paper, alongside Kristal and Whillans.
PNAS published the retraction notice on 13 September 2021.

follow.q: Why did a failed replication matter so much?
follow.a: The authors note that government agencies had adopted the practice, so they argued the scientific record needed updating.

challenges.title: When salaries go public
challenges.scene: A new website published University of California employees' pay. Researchers told a random subset of staff about the site, then surveyed everyone on job satisfaction and job search.
challenges.question: What did learning about peers' pay do?
options: Below-median earners: less satisfied, job hunting
No change: staff already knew peer pay
challenges.answerTitle: Below-median earners grew unhappy and started looking
challenges.explain: Workers paid below the median for their unit and occupation reported lower pay and job satisfaction and were more likely to look for a new job. Above-median earners were unaffected.
challenges.implication: Before publishing pay data, prepare clear explanations of pay differences for below-median staff, who carry the morale cost.
challenges.boundary: University of California employees; outcomes were self-reported satisfaction and job-search intentions.

dag.alt: A random notice about the website changes who knows peers' pay, which affects satisfaction. Unobserved traits such as ability and fit drive both pay rank and satisfaction, which is why a simple survey correlation between rank and satisfaction is confounded.

follow.q: Why randomize who heard about the site?
follow.a: Low-paid staff differ from high-paid staff in many ways. Randomizing who learned about the site isolates the effect of the information itself.

follow.q: Did higher earners gain from learning they earn more?
follow.a: No. Workers paid above the median were unaffected.

follow.q: Does pay level or pay rank matter more?
follow.a: Rank. The authors conclude that differences in pay rank matter more than differences in pay levels.

challenges.title: Unequal pay, lower output
challenges.scene: For a month, Indian manufacturing workers in production teams were randomly paid either the same flat daily wage or different wages based on their baseline productivity rank.
challenges.question: Is this what the study found?
challenges.answerTitle: Output fell 0.45 SD; attendance fell 18 points
challenges.explain: When coworkers' productivity was difficult to observe, pay inequality reduced output by 0.45 standard deviations and attendance by 18 percentage points, and weakened cooperation.
challenges.implication: If pay differs within a team, make the productivity basis visible to everyone before the gap takes effect.
challenges.boundary: When workers clearly saw that higher-paid peers were more productive, pay gaps had no discernible effect.

follow.a: No. When workers could clearly perceive that higher-paid peers were more productive, pay disparity had no discernible effect on output, attendance or group cohesion.
Pay inequality also lowered coworkers' ability to cooperate in their own self-interest.

follow.q: How long did the experiment run?
follow.a: About one month, in Indian manufacturing.

forecast.claim: Where coworkers could not easily see who was more productive, paying them unequal wages raised output.

challenges.title: Compare candidates, not impressions
challenges.scene: Evaluators chose workers for a task and were paid on the chosen worker's future performance. Some saw candidates one at a time; others compared candidates side by side.
challenges.question: Which procedure made evaluators rely more on individual performance?
options: Seeing candidates one at a time
challenges.answerTitle: Side-by-side review focused choices on performance
challenges.explain: Evaluators were more likely to base decisions on individual performance in joint than in separate evaluation, where they leaned more on group stereotypes, making joint evaluation the profit-maximizing procedure.
challenges.implication: Compare shortlisted candidates side by side on the same criteria instead of scoring each one in isolation.
challenges.boundary: Incentivized lab hiring task with clear performance scores; real hiring information is noisier.

follow.a: The authors draw on decision research showing that people reason more carefully when they compare options together than when they judge one in isolation.

follow.q: Does it cost the employer anything?
follow.a: No. Because evaluators picked on performance, joint evaluation was the profit-maximizing procedure.

follow.q: How does it relate to blind auditions?
follow.a: The authors present it as an alternative to blind evaluation, which helped women musicians win orchestra positions but is hard to use in many workplaces.

challenges.title: The default decides
challenges.scene: An online survey asked 161 people whether they would be organ donors. The question was framed as opt-in, opt-out, or a neutral form requiring a choice with no default.
challenges.question: Which two forms produced similarly high consent?
challenges.answerTitle: Opt-out and active choice both beat opt-in
challenges.explain: Consent was about twice as high under opt-out as under opt-in, and opt-out did not differ significantly from the neutral form (79%).
challenges.implication: Where you cannot set a favorable default, require an active choice rather than leaving opt-in as the silent default.
challenges.boundary: Stated intentions from 161 online respondents; the country comparisons in the paper are correlational.

follow.q: Does this show up across countries?
follow.a: Yes. In effective consent rates, nearly 60 percentage points separated opt-out from opt-in European countries, with no overlap.
In a 1999 cross-section cited by the authors, presumed-consent countries had 16.9 donations per million versus 10.8 in explicit-consent countries.

follow.q: Why does the default matter so much?
follow.a: The authors argue that if preferences about donation were strong, defaults should have little effect; the large gap suggests many people hold weak preferences.

challenges.title: The menu picks the portfolio
challenges.scene: Your 401(k) offers five funds. Menu X has four stock funds and one bond fund. Menu Y has one stock fund and four bond funds.
challenges.question: How will employees' stock exposure differ between the two menus?
options: Same: people pick their own risk level
challenges.answerTitle: Stock share follows the menu
challenges.explain: Some investors divide contributions evenly across the funds offered, so the proportion invested in stocks depends strongly on the proportion of stock funds in the plan.
challenges.implication: Audit the mix of fund types on your plan menu, because it quietly sets employees' risk exposure.
challenges.boundary: Not every investor splits evenly; the evidence combines hypothetical allocation tasks with plan-level data.

follow.a: Dividing contributions evenly across whatever funds the plan offers, regardless of what those funds hold.
No. The paper finds that some investors follow it, which is enough to shift average stock exposure.

follow.q: Does it show up in real plans?
follow.a: Yes. The authors report that the proportion invested in stocks depends strongly on the proportion of stock funds in the plan.

challenges.title: The wallet with more cash
challenges.scene: Researchers handed 'lost' wallets to staff at banks, hotels, post offices and police stations. In the US, UK and Poland, wallets held no money, US$13.45, or US$94.15.
challenges.question: Rank the wallets by how often staff contacted the owner.
challenges.rankLabel: Share of wallets reported to the owner
challenges.answerTitle: More money, more wallets returned
challenges.explain: Reporting rose from 46% with no money to 61% with US$13.45 and 72% with US$94.15. Across all 40 countries, money raised reporting from 40% to 51%.
challenges.implication: When designing controls, make the owner and the stakes visible; people resist taking more when it would clearly feel like theft.
challenges.boundary: Wallets handed to counter staff in 355 cities; return was measured by owner emails, a measure later questioned for cross-country rankings.

follow.q: Did the key in the wallet matter?
follow.a: Yes. In the US, UK and Poland, wallets with a key were 9.2 percentage points more likely to be reported, which the authors read as concern for the owner.

follow.q: Did this hold in every country?
follow.a: The money effect appeared in 38 of 40 countries, and no country showed a significant drop in reporting when money was added.
17,303 wallets were turned in across 355 cities in 40 countries, typically five to eight of each country's largest cities.

challenges.title: What the experts expected
challenges.scene: Before the wallet results were public, researchers asked 279 US economists and 299 US laypeople how adding cash to a lost wallet would change return rates.
challenges.question: Did most economists foresee that more cash means more returns?

forecast.claim: Most surveyed economists predicted that more money in a wallet would raise return rates.

challenges.answerTitle: Only 29% of economists predicted the increase
challenges.explain: Among 279 economists, 49% predicted a decrease and 29% an increase; among 299 laypeople only 18% predicted the increase that actually occurred.
challenges.implication: Pilot honesty controls before scaling them; expert intuition about how people respond to temptation got the direction wrong here.
challenges.boundary: Predictions came from US survey samples; actual behavior came from the 40-country field experiment with wallets handed to counter staff.

follow.a: They expected reporting to fall as money increased, from 73% with no money to 65% with a modest sum and 55% with a substantial sum.
Their errors were smaller, but they predicted roughly flat rates of 69%, 69% and 66% rather than the rise that occurred.
In the US, UK and Poland, reporting rose from 46% with no money to 61% with US$13.45 and 72% with US$94.15.

challenges.title: How much do people lie?
challenges.scene: Across 90 experiments, people privately rolled a die or flipped a coin and reported the result. Higher reports paid more, and nobody could check.
challenges.question: What share of the possible gains from lying did people leave on the table?

estimate.label: Share of potential lying gains forgone

challenges.answerTitle: About three-quarters of possible gains forgone
challenges.explain: Pooling 270,616 decisions by 44,390 subjects, the average standardized report was only 0.234: subjects forgo about three-quarters of the potential gains from lying.
challenges.implication: For self-reported claims such as expenses or hours, assume most people report honestly and aim checks at the minority who inflate.
challenges.boundary: Lab and online reporting tasks with modest stakes; raising incentives changed behavior very little within these studies.

follow.q: Why do people pass up free money?
follow.a: The authors' new experiments point to two main motives: a preference for being honest and a preference for being seen as honest.

follow.q: Do bigger stakes produce more lying?
follow.a: Barely. Subjects continued to refrain from lying maximally when stakes increased, and incentives affected behavior only very little.

follow.q: How large is the evidence base?
follow.a: 90 experimental studies from economics, psychology and sociology, covering 270,616 decisions by 44,390 subjects.

challenges.title: Honest, liar, or in between
challenges.scene: Lab participants rolled a die in private and reported the number for cash. Nobody could verify any individual roll.
challenges.question: What share of participants did researchers estimate were fully honest?

estimate.label: Estimated share of honest participants

challenges.answerTitle: About 39% honest, at most 22% full liars
challenges.explain: The authors estimate that 39% of subjects were honest and at most 22% lied completely; others lied without maximizing their income.
challenges.implication: Design expense or time reporting so moderate inflation, not only extreme claims, meets a check or a reminder.
challenges.boundary: One-shot lab die task; the shares are inferred from the distribution of reports, not from observing any individual's lie.

follow.q: How can they know who lied?
follow.a: They cannot see individual rolls. They compare the distribution of reports with what a fair die produces, which bounds the shares of honest and fully dishonest people.
The authors point to a wish to keep a favorable self-image, including being seen as honest and not greedy.

follow.q: Why does partial lying matter for managers?
follow.a: Because some people lie without maximizing income, controls that only flag the most extreme claims miss part of the dishonesty the study documents.

challenges.title: Corruption and the die cup
challenges.scene: Students in 23 countries rolled a die twice in a cup and were paid for reporting the first roll. Their countries differed in corruption, tax evasion and political fraud.
challenges.question: Where did the extra dishonesty in high-violation countries come from?

forecast.claim: In high rule-violation societies, the extra dishonesty came mainly from people claiming the maximum payoff.

challenges.answerTitle: More rule-bending, not more maximal cheating
challenges.explain: Mean claims were 3.17 in low-violation pools and 3.53 in high-violation pools, near the 3.47 'justified dishonesty' benchmark; the share claiming the maximum was unrelated to rule violations.
challenges.implication: Where rule-breaking is common, expect small self-justified stretching more than brazen fraud; remove ambiguity people use to rationalize.
challenges.boundary: 2,568 students in 23 countries; a cross-society correlation measured years after the country index, not a causal test of institutions.

follow.a: Reporting the higher of the two rolls instead of the first, a self-justifiable lie. Its benchmark average is 3.47, close to the 3.53 claimed in high-violation societies.

follow.q: How many people were fully honest?
follow.a: An estimated 48.9% on average, ranging from 4.3% to 87% across subject pools, with fewer fully honest people in high-violation societies.
A country index combining political fraud, tax evasion and corruption, based on data from 2003; the experiments ran at least eight years later.

challenges.title: One sentence in a tax letter
challenges.scene: The UK tax authority sent reminder letters to over 200,000 people with overdue tax. Letters varied one added message: social norms, public services, or loss versus gain framing.
challenges.question: Which two findings did these field experiments report?
options: Social norm messages raised payment rates
challenges.answerTitle: Norm and public-services lines raised payments
challenges.explain: Across more than 200,000 UK taxpayers, adding social norm messages to standard reminders increased payment of overdue tax; public-services messages also helped, and loss framing did no better.
challenges.implication: In compliance reminders, state accurately what most peers do and what the money funds, and test wording on real payment data.
challenges.boundary: UK taxpayers with overdue Self Assessment debts; outcomes were short-run payment, which accelerated revenue rather than proving lasting compliance.

follow.q: Which kind of norm worked better?
follow.a: Descriptive norms, which state what most people do, appeared more effective than injunctive norms about what people ought to do.
No. The authors found no evidence that loss framing is more effective than gain framing.
No. The authors report that the experiments accelerated the collection of tax revenue at little cost.

challenges.title: Follow the other side
challenges.scene: Researchers paid frequent Twitter users who identified as Democrats or Republicans to follow, for one month, a bot retweeting elected officials and opinion leaders from the other party.
challenges.question: Did a month of opposing views moderate Republicans?

forecast.claim: Republicans who followed a liberal bot became more conservative afterward.

challenges.answerTitle: Republicans moved right; Democrats barely moved
challenges.explain: For Republicans the intent-to-treat effect was 0.12 points toward conservatism on a seven-point scale, rising to 0.60 among full compliers; the Democrats' shift was small and not significant.
challenges.implication: Do not expect that feeding a divided team the other side's messages builds understanding; structure direct, cooperative contact instead.
challenges.boundary: Party-identified US adults using Twitter at least three times weekly, paid to follow a bot for one month in late 2017.

follow.a: 1,652 respondents were recruited (901 Democrats, 751 Republicans); 697 Democrats and 542 Republicans were analyzed.
They became slightly more liberal, but the intent-to-treat effect of 0.02 points was not statistically significant.
The authors could not identify the mechanism. They discuss more political exposure, exposure to women and minority voices, and an anti-elite reaction as possibilities.

challenges.title: Four weeks without Facebook
challenges.scene: Before the 2018 US midterm election, researchers randomly paid some Facebook users to deactivate their accounts for four weeks and compared them with users who kept using it.
challenges.question: Which two effects did deactivation produce?
challenges.answerTitle: Less polarized and happier, but less informed
challenges.explain: Deactivation lowered the polarization index by 0.16 standard deviations and raised well-being by 0.09, but news knowledge fell by 0.19.
challenges.implication: Before limiting staff social media, weigh gains in mood and calmer politics against lower awareness of current news.
challenges.boundary: Four weeks of paid deactivation among US Facebook users recruited through ads, in the run-up to a national election.

chart.note: Values reported in Allcott et al. (2020), introduction (authors' final manuscript); effects in standard deviations, treatment minus control.

follow.q: How much time did it free up?
follow.a: Deactivating Facebook freed up about 60 minutes per day for the average person in the treatment group.

follow.q: Did people go back to Facebook afterward?
follow.a: Less than before: post-experiment Facebook use was 0.61 standard deviations lower in treatment than in control.

follow.q: What did people need to be paid?
follow.a: The median willingness to accept to deactivate for four weeks was $100; the mean was $180.

challenges.title: One question before sharing
challenges.scene: Researchers sent 5,379 Twitter users a private message asking them to rate the accuracy of a single non-political headline, then tracked the news they shared.
challenges.question: Did one accuracy question improve what people shared?

forecast.claim: The single accuracy prompt raised the average quality of news users shared.

challenges.answerTitle: A small but real lift in quality
challenges.explain: On days users tweeted, the average quality of shared news rose 4.8%; counting all user-days, the gain was 2.1%.
challenges.implication: Add a light accuracy prompt before staff forward external content internally, and expect modest rather than dramatic gains.
challenges.boundary: One private message on Twitter; gains were a few percent, and a replication of the authors' earlier survey version found weaker effects.

follow.q: Why would people share news they doubt?
follow.a: In the survey studies, headline truth had little effect on sharing intentions despite a large effect on accuracy judgments; the authors argue attention is focused elsewhere.

follow.q: What happened in the survey experiments?
follow.a: Discernment between true and false headlines in sharing was 2.0 times larger with the prompt in Study 3 and 2.4 times larger in Study 4.
Partly. A preregistered replication of the authors' 2020 study failed at its first stage and found only a small effect after more data (Roozenbeek et al. 2021).

study.design: Field experiment on Twitter plus survey experiments

challenges.title: Who spreads the falsehood
challenges.scene: Researchers traced about 126,000 fact-checked true and false stories that roughly 3 million Twitter users shared more than 4.5 million times between 2006 and 2017.
challenges.question: What explains why false stories spread faster than true ones?
options: Bots pushed false stories harder than true ones
People shared false stories more than true ones
False stories spread no faster overall
Only false political stories spread faster
challenges.answerTitle: People, not bots, drove the faster spread
challenges.explain: Across about 126,000 stories, falsehood spread farther and faster in all categories; bots accelerated true and false news at the same rate, so humans drove the gap.
challenges.implication: Counter workplace rumors by addressing human sharing, such as fast, specific official updates, rather than relying on filtering automated accounts.
challenges.boundary: Twitter from 2006 to 2017, stories verified by fact-checkers; it describes diffusion patterns and tests no intervention.

follow.q: Which topics showed the largest gap?
follow.a: The effects were more pronounced for false political news than for other categories of information.

follow.q: Why might people share falsehoods more?
follow.a: False news was more novel than true news, and the authors suggest people are more likely to share novel information.
Bots accelerated true and false news at the same rate, so they did not explain why falsehood outran the truth.

challenges.title: The silent majority in Riyadh
challenges.scene: Researchers anonymously asked 500 married Saudi men aged 18 to 35 whether women should be allowed to work outside the home, and to guess how many peers agreed.
challenges.question: What share of the men privately agreed?

estimate.label: Share privately supporting women working outside the home

challenges.answerTitle: 87% agreed, but guessed only 63% of peers did
challenges.explain: 87% agreed, yet on average they guessed that 63% of other session participants agreed; 72% underestimated support, by 24 points on average.
challenges.implication: Before assuming a change lacks support, poll private views anonymously and share the actual numbers with the group.
challenges.boundary: 500 married men aged 18 to 35 in Riyadh, in sessions of about 30; beliefs concerned other men in the same session.

follow.q: Were men just telling researchers what they wanted?
follow.a: Unlikely. A list experiment in a national survey found 80% support versus 82% by direct question, suggesting little social desirability bias.

follow.q: What happened when men learned the true figure?
follow.a: In the control group 23.5% chose to sign their wives up for a job-matching service; with the information, 32.0% did.
Yes. Prentice and Miller (1993) found students believed they were more uncomfortable with campus drinking than the average student.

challenges.title: From belief to job applications
challenges.scene: Saudi husbands who underestimated peers' support for women working outside the home were shown the true figure. Months later, researchers checked whether their wives had applied for outside jobs.
challenges.question: What happened to wives' job applications three to five months later?
options: No change: beliefs moved, behavior did not
challenges.answerTitle: Applications nearly tripled, 5.8% to 16.2%
challenges.explain: Wives of informed men applied for outside jobs at 16.2% versus 5.8%, and interviewed at 5.8% versus 1.1%.
challenges.implication: Share accurate peer-support data to move stalled behavior, then track actual outcomes for months, not just stated intentions.
